questions.prompt: Towels are low, a client is waiting, and a colleague starts asking who forgot the laundry. What should come first?
options: Name the person at fault so accountability is protected.
Get the client attended to with a practical option, then later understand why it happened. Resolution should come before unnecessary blame.
Offer an unauthorized discount for the delay.
Tell the client it is reception's culture problem.

questions.prompt: A small spill is in your space and within your duty. You wait for a leader to assign it. What did you confuse?
options: Initiative with overstepping. Reasonable action now is still problem-solving.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a discount because the room was late. You want to be a problem-solver. What must you not do?
options: Stay calm and escalate money decisions.
Promise a refund or unauthorized discount to “fix it yourself.”
Protect the client's experience while the internal issue is handled.

questions.prompt: You hide a client complaint because you fear accountability. What does the standard say happens next?
options: The problem disappears if the client leaves smiling.
Hidden problems usually become larger problems later.
Hiding complaints is required until you have a full investigation.

questions.prompt: The preferred room is still being cleaned. Which report is the standard's useful version?
options: “The preferred room is still being cleaned. We can use Room 2 now so the client is not delayed.”
“I will change company policy on room assignment.”

questions.prompt: A colleague made a room-prep mistake. What is the healthiest team line?
options: Help protect the client, solve the immediate problem, then understand why it happened — without “Who can I blame?”
Humiliate them in the corridor so it never happens again.
Hide the mistake so nobody feels uncomfortable.

questions.prompt: You report a broken massage gun, then walk away while the client is still on the table and your involvement is still needed. What is missing?
options: Resolve or hand over properly. Do not simply report and leave if your involvement is still necessary.

questions.prompt: You become loud and insulting as soon as a scheduling mix-up appears. Why is this a poor response even if you are “passionate”?
options: Anger as the first response usually makes the problem harder to solve.
Loudness is required so management notices.
The client should hear every internal disagreement.
Insults are acceptable if you later solve it.

questions.prompt: A serious safety issue appears. You try to “solve everything alone” because you have a problem-solving mindset. What did you miss?
options: Problem-solving means you must never escalate.
Sometimes the correct solution is report, ask for help, or escalate. Judgment is knowing initiative from overstepping.
Safety issues should wait until after the massage.

questions.prompt: After the client is recovered, you still do not ask why the room failed. What sequence did you stop too early?
options: Stabilize → solve the immediate problem → understand the cause → address responsibility → prevent recurrence.

title: SECTION B — FILL IN THE GAP

questions.prompt: Complete the article: “You may not control the problem, but you are responsible for _____.”
Complete the Zura problem-solving standard line: “NOTICE → PAUSE → UNDERSTAND → PRIORITIZE → ACT → COMMUNICATE → ESCALATE → RESOLVE → _____.”
Complete: “The therapist should avoid immediately asking ‘Who caused this?’ The first questions should be: ‘What happened?’ ‘What needs to happen now?’ ‘What can I do?’ ‘_____?’”
Complete: “A problem should not automatically become an argument, a complaint session, a blame game, gossip, or _____."
Complete: “The purpose is not ‘Who can I blame?’ It is: ‘How do we protect the client, solve the problem, and _____?’”
Near the opening, what is the expected inner response when a problem occurs — not “Something is wrong” or “This person caused it”?
options: “Who failed, and how do we expose them?”
“What is the actual problem, what can I responsibly do about it, and who needs to be involved if it is beyond my responsibility?”
“Problems must never happen if we are professional.”
“I must personally solve every problem without help.”

questions.prompt: The article says a therapist who can massage well but cannot respond constructively when something goes wrong…
options: is still fully competent because technique is everything.
can still negatively affect the client's experience; problem-solving is part of professional competence.

questions.prompt: Section 11 warns that a problem-solving mindset does not mean…
In the accountability sequence, if a client is waiting because the room is not ready, what comes first?
options: Determine why the room failed, then attend the client.
First get the client properly attended to. Then afterwards determine why the room was not ready.
Write a disciplinary note before anyone enters.

questions.prompt: The closing of the standard says seeing a problem and only complaining about it is…
options: enough, if the complaint is loud.
